raw.title: Google Appscript(V8) function does not stop execution after return statement
raw.body:
thanks in advance for any replies

Currently writing a small script to be utilized in a mileage sheet I'm making to track miles for my tax return. I've written a function that I intend to utilize on each cell in a column to return to the cell a value of either true or false.

Currently my function runs. Doesn't give any syntax errors and through debug and logging I've determined that it reaches my return statements and functions as expected. Main issue is that it will hang once it reaches the statement until it eventually throws an error for exceeding maximum execution time.

I primarily write c++ and python on the day to day but have done some js/appscript and vba for excel in the past with little to no issue and don't see why exactly this isn't working as it's a very simple procedure. Last time I wrote app script it was prior to V8 so I'm assuming it's something I'm naive to.

Here's the code:


// region Logging:
const logSeperator = "--------------------------------\n";
// endregion

//region Constants

const VacationDays = [
  new Date("1/1/25"),
  new Date("1/20/25"),
  new Date("2/17/25"),
  new Date("5/26/25"),
  new Date("6/19/25"),
  new Date("7/4/25"),
  new Date("7/4/25"),
  new Date("9/1/25"),
  new Date("10/13/25"),
  new Date("11/11/25"),
  new Date("11/27/25"),
  new Date("12/25/25"),
  new Date("12/26/25"),
  new Date("12/27/25"),
  new Date("12/31/25"),
];

// endregion

function tryReinterpretAsDate(targetObject){
  console.log(Object.prototype.toString.call(targetObject))
  if (Object.prototype.toString.call(targetObject) == "[object Date]"){
    return new Date(targetObject);
  }
  return targetObject;
}

function ISWORKDAY(targetCell = 'A11') {
  const ss = SpreadsheetApp.getActive();
  const sheet = ss.getSheetByName("Sheet1");
  console.log('Target Date Cell: %s', targetCell);
  const _range = sheet.getRange(targetCell);
  let val = tryReinterpretAsDate(_range.getValue());
  const isDate = val instanceof Date;
  console.log(`${logSeperator}Target Cell \nType: ${isDate} \nValue: ${val}\n${logSeperator}`);

  if(isDate){
    console.log("Target value is Date");
    const dayOfWeek = val.getDay();

    if (VacationDays.includes(val) || [0, 6].includes(dayOfWeek)){
      console.log("Target value is a non work day... Returning false");
      return "false";
    };

    console.log("Target value is a work day... Returning true");
    return "true";
  }
  return "false"

};

And some example output:

3:06:27 AM Notice Execution started
3:06:27 AM Info Target Date Cell: A11
3:06:27 AM Info [object Date]
3:06:27 AM Info
--------------------------------
Target Cell 
Type: true 
Value: Sun Jun 15 2025 00:00:00 GMT-0400 (Eastern Daylight Time)
--------------------------------
3:06:27 AM Info Target value is Date
3:06:27 AM Info Target value is a non work day... Returning false
3:12:27 AM Error Exceeded maximum execution time

In my sheet I set a given cell equal to =ISWORKDAY("A11") And get #ERROR: Exceeded maximum execution time (line 0).

items.title: alive/issues #35: Leverage SDK 0.2.34 capabilities
items.content:
## Context

We upgraded `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` from 0.1.60 to 0.2.34 in the `codex/sdk-0-2-34-full-audit` branch. The upgrade is done, but we're not yet using the new capabilities it unlocks.

## 1. `Query.close()` — Force-terminate stuck queries

**Added in:** 0.2.15

**Current state:** Cancellation uses `AbortController` + `AbortSignal`. Worker sets up `currentAbortController` per query and passes `signal` to `query()` options. On cancel, calls `.abort()`.

**Where it matters:**
- `packages/worker-pool/src/worker-entry.mjs:528-529` — AbortController setup
- `apps/web/app/api/claude/stream/route.ts:308-328` — Cancel callback registration
- Worker pool has 500ms cleanup timeout for unresponsive workers

**What's missing:** No forced termination for truly stuck queries (e.g. MCP server hangs, infinite tool loops). `maxTurns` is the only guard (`route.ts:387`). `Query.close()` would give a hard kill switch.

**Action:**
- [ ] Add admin "kill conversation" capability using `Query.close()`
- [ ] Use as fallback when `AbortController.abort()` doesn't resolve within timeout

## 2. `stop_reason` on results — Know why the model stopped

**Added in:** 0.2.31

**Current state:** The codebase does NOT inspect `stop_reason`. It only checks for `error_max_turns` subtype in `ResultMessage.tsx:11-14`. All other failures show generic "I encountered an error while streaming my response" with an Error ID.

**Where it matters:**
- `apps/web/features/chat/components/message-renderers/ResultMessage.tsx` — Only handles `error_max_turns`
- `packages/worker-pool/src/worker-entry.mjs:715-717` — Captures `result` but doesn't log `stop_reason`
- `apps/web/e2e-tests/lib/stream-builder.ts:86,116,148` — Test fixtures hardcode `stop_reason: "end_turn"` and `"tool_use"` but no test coverage for other reasons

**What users see vs could see:**
| Now | With stop_reason |
|-----|-----------------|
| "Error while streaming" | "Conversation hit turn limit. Summarize or start fresh." |
| "Error while streaming" | "A tool failed during execution." |
| "Error while streaming" | "Request cancelled." |

**Action:**
- [ ] Parse `stop_reason` in result handler for context-specific UI messages
- [ ] Log `stop_reason` in worker for backend debugging
- [ ] Add test coverage for all stop reason variants

## 3. Debug logging — `debug` and `debugFile` options

**Added in:** 0.2.30

**Current state:** Worker captures `stderr` from Claude subprocess (worker-entry.mjs:669-675), buffers up to 50 lines, and includes it in error responses. `logStreamError()` writes `STREAM_ERROR:<requestId>` to journalctl. No SDK-level debug output.

**Where it matters:**
- `packages/worker-pool/src/worker-entry.mjs:669-696` — stderr handler
- `apps/web/lib/error-logger.ts:200-240` — `logStreamError()` 
- `docs/troubleshooting/stream-errors.md` — Current debug workflow

**Action:**
- [ ] Enable `debug: true` when `STREAM_ENV=local` for richer dev logs
- [ ] Add `debugFile: "/var/log/claude-bridge/debug-${requestId}.log"` option for per-request debug in production
- [ ] Could be toggled via admin setting for on-demand production debugging

## 4. MCP server management — `reconnectMcpServer()`, `toggleMcpServer()`

**Added in:** 0.2.21

**Current state:** MCP servers are created fresh on EVERY query (worker-entry.mjs:640-658). No persistent connections, no reconnection, no health checks. Three server types:
1. **SDK Internal** (`createSdkMcpServer`): alive-workspace, alive-tools, supabase
2. **Global HTTP**: from `GLOBAL_MCP_PROVIDERS` in `@webalive/shared`
3. **OAuth HTTP**: stripe, gmail, linear, etc. (from user OAuth connections)

If any MCP server fails mid-query, the query errors out with no retry.

**Action:**
- [ ] Evaluate persistent MCP server pool (reuse HTTP connections across queries)
- [ ] Add `reconnectMcpServer()` on connection failures
- [ ] Monitor MCP server health with `mcpServerStatus()` (now includes `config`, `scope`, `tools`, `disabled` fields)

## 5. Zod v4 peer dep — Audit monorepo compatibility

**Current state:** SDK peers on `zod ^4.0.0`. Zod is imported in 30+ files across packages including:
- `packages/env/src/schema.ts` — Environment validation
- `apps/web/types/guards/api.ts` — API request validation
- `packages/oauth-core/src/config.ts` — OAuth config schemas
- `packages/alrighty/src/client.ts` — API client validation
- `packages/tools/src/tools/*/` — MCP tool input schemas

**Action:**
- [ ] Verify single zod version resolves across all packages (`bun pm ls | grep zod`)
- [ ] Check for v3 API patterns that changed in v4

## 6. Lower-priority gains

- [ ] **PDF page reading** (0.2.30) — `pages` field on `FileReadToolInput`. Free capability.
- [ ] **Tool annotations** (0.2.27) — `annotations` on `tool()` for MCP hints (`readOnlyHint`, `destructiveHint`). Could improve tool selection.
- [ ] **Notification hooks** (0.2.15) — Hook support for notifications.

## References
- Audit report: `docs/reports/sdk-upgrades/anthropic-sdk-0.2.34-audit.md`
- Changelog span: `docs/reports/sdk-upgrades/anthropic-sdk-0.2.34-changelog-span.md`
- Impact matrix: `docs/reports/sdk-upgrades/anthropic-sdk-0.2.34-impact-matrix.csv`

items.title: opencode/issues #12666: Startup shows blank screen for several seconds when plugins are configured
items.content:
## Description

When plugins (especially oh-my-opencode or other npm-based plugins) are configured, opencode startup takes several seconds with **no visual feedback** — just a blank black screen. This makes users think the application is frozen or their computer is stuck.

## Root cause

The startup delay comes from multiple sequential blocking operations that happen before the TUI renders:

1. `getTerminalBackgroundColor()` blocks up to 1000ms querying the terminal
2. `InstanceBootstrap` runs lazily on the first API request, which includes:
   - `Plugin.init()` — installs plugins from npm (`bun add`) one by one, each acquiring a write lock
   - `LSP.init()` — spawns language server processes
   - `FileWatcher.init()`, `Vcs.init()`, etc.
3. TUI-side `sync.tsx` bootstrap fetches providers, agents, config from the server

All of this happens with zero user feedback.

## Expected behavior

Users should see what's happening during startup — a splash screen with progress logs showing each initialization step (plugin install, LSP init, etc.).

## Environment

- opencode with oh-my-opencode and other plugins configured
- macOS / Linux terminal

items.title: openclaw/issues #11687: Feature Request: Support OpenRouter 'user' parameter for per-user/agent tracking
items.content:
## Summary

Add support for passing the OpenRouter `user` parameter in API requests, allowing users to track usage per end-user or per-agent.

## Background

OpenRouter's API accepts a `user` field in the request body:

```typescript
user?: string; // A stable identifier for your end-users. Used to help detect and prevent abuse.
```

This is useful for:
- Tracking API usage per agent in multi-agent setups
- Abuse detection and rate limiting by user
- Cost attribution in the OpenRouter dashboard

## Current State

- OpenClaw's config schema has a `params` field under `agents.defaults.models.<modelId>` that's a free-form object
- However, this doesn't appear to be passed through to the provider API request body
- No `extraBody` or similar mechanism exists in the gateway config schema

## Proposed Solution

Either:
1. Pass the `params` field from model config through to the API request body
2. Add an `extraBody` config option at the provider or model level
3. Add a specific `user` field for OpenRouter-compatible providers

## Use Case

Multi-agent setup where each agent should be trackable separately in OpenRouter's usage dashboard.

## Environment

- OpenClaw version: 2026.2.6-3
- Provider: OpenRouter
- Model: openrouter/anthropic/claude-opus-4.5

  "abstract": "Recently, rubrics have been used to guide LLM judges in capturing subjective, nuanced, multi-dimensional human preferences, and have been extended from evaluation to reward signals for reinforcement fine-tuning (RFT). However, rubric generation remains hard to control: rubrics often lack coverage, conflate dimensions, misalign preference direction, and contain redundant or highly correlated criteria, degrading judge accuracy and producing suboptimal rewards during RFT. We propose RRD, a principled framework for rubric refinement built on a recursive decompose-filter cycle. RRD decomposes coarse rubrics into fine-grained, discriminative criteria, expanding coverage while sharpening separation between responses. A complementary filtering mechanism removes misaligned and redundant rubrics, and a correlation-aware weighting scheme prevents over-representing highly correlated criteria, yielding rubric sets that are informative, comprehensive, and non-redundant. Empirically, RRD delivers large, consistent gains across both evaluation and training: it improves preference-judgment accuracy on JudgeBench and PPE for both GPT-4o and Llama3.1-405B judges, achieving top performance in all settings with up to +17.7 points on JudgeBench. When used as the reward source for RFT on WildChat, it yields substantially stronger and more stable learning signals, boosting reward by up to 160% (Qwen3-4B) and 60% (Llama3.1-8B) versus 10-20% for prior rubric baselines, with gains that transfer to HealthBench-Hard and BiGGen Bench. Overall, RRD establishes recursive rubric refinement as a scalable and interpretable foundation for LLM judging and reward modeling in open-ended domains.",

items.title: loa-finn/issues #31: RFC: The Hounfour — Multi-Model Provider Abstraction, Cloud Deployment & Agent Distribution
items.content:
# RFC: The Hounfour — Multi-Model Provider Abstraction, Cloud Deployment & Agent Distribution

**Status:** Draft v4 — Implementation-Ready (blocking fixes applied)  
**Author:** Jani  
**Date:** 2026-02-08  
**Revision:** v3 addressed operational items; v4 fixes five blocking correctness issues from final review  
**Scope:** Loa Framework → loa-finn Runtime → Arrakis Distribution  
**References:** [finnNFT #27](https://github.com/0xHoneyJar/loa-finn/issues/27) · [Bridgebuilder #24](https://github.com/0xHoneyJar/loa-finn/issues/24) · [OpenCode Config](https://opencode.ai/docs/config/)

---

## Preamble: Why This Document Exists

> *"The difference between a junior engineer and a senior engineer is that the junior asks 'does it work?' and the senior asks 'what happens when it works at scale, for 10,000 users, at 3am, when the primary model provider is down?'"*

Three systems are converging:

1. **Loa** — an AI agent-driven development framework with 8 specialized agents, currently coupled to Claude Code as both runtime and model.
2. **loa-finn** — an OpenCode-like service that gives Loa a server runtime: persistent sessions, scheduled behaviors, compound learning, and a tool sandbox. Think of it as the engine block.
3. **Arrakis** — a token-gated community management platform spanning Discord and Telegram. Think of it as the highway system.

The vision: Loa agents run inside loa-finn, served to users through Arrakis, powered by whichever model backend is cheapest, fastest, or most capable for the task. A finnNFT holder talks to their daemon companion — and behind the scenes, the personality prompt routes to Qwen3-Coder-Next for a quick code fix, Kimi-K2-Thinking for deep multi-step reasoning, or Claude for architecture decisions. The user never knows. The NFT doesn't care. The wallet just sees a bill.

This RFC defines the complete architecture for that future: from the provider abstraction in Loa, through the cloud deployment in loa-finn, to the metered distribution through Arrakis.

---

## Table of Contents

1. [The Problem](#1-the-problem)
2. [Architecture Overview](#2-architecture-overview)
3. [Model Catalog](#3-model-catalog)
4. [Prior Art & What We're Stealing](#4-prior-art--what-were-stealing)
5. [Provider Abstraction Layer](#5-provider-abstraction-layer)
    - 5.1 The ModelPort Interface
    - 5.2 Execution Modes
    - 5.3 Tool Calling Contract
    - 5.4 Capability Matrix
    - 5.5 Adapter Implementations
    - 5.6 Skill Decomposition for Portability
6. [Configuration Schema](#6-configuration-schema)
    - 6.1 Naming Rules
    - 6.2 Precedence & Merge Semantics
    - 6.3 The Full Config Schema
    - 6.4 Routing: Fallback & Downgrade
7. [Adapter Implementation](#7-adapter-implementation)
    - 7.1 model-invoke (shell orchestrator)
    - 7.2 cheval.py (Python adapter core)
    - 7.3 File Map
8. [Cloud Deployment](#8-cloud-deployment)
9. [Metering, Billing & Cost Attribution](#9-metering-billing--cost-attribution)
10. [Data Retention, Privacy & Thinking Trace Policy](#10-data-retention-privacy--thinking-trace-policy)
11. [Security & Multi-Tenant Hardening](#11-security--multi-tenant-hardening)
12. [Agent Distribution via Arrakis](#12-agent-distribution-via-arrakis)
13. [Repo Ownership](#13-repo-ownership)
14. [Implementation Phases](#14-implementation-phases)
15. [Design Decisions & Rationale](#15-design-decisions--rationale)
16. [Open Questions](#16-open-questions)
17. [Success Criteria](#17-success-criteria)
18. [Naming & Mythology](#18-naming--mythology)

---

## 1. The Problem

Loa is currently a one-model framework. Every agent — from the requirements discoverer to the security auditor — runs on Claude Code. The GPT integration in the Flatline Protocol is ad-hoc, bolted on with direct API calls rather than flowing through a principled abstraction.

This creates three problems:

**The vendor lock problem.** If Anthropic's API goes down, every agent goes down. If pricing doubles, every agent's cost doubles. Google learned this with their early dependence on a single ad-serving stack — when they finally built the Universal Second Price auction to abstract across formats, revenue diversification followed. We need our agents to be model-portable.

**The cost problem.** Claude Opus at $75/1M output tokens is a Lamborghini. Beautiful, but you don't drive it to the grocery store. Some tasks — summarizing a sprint for executives, generating a quick unit test — need a Honda Civic. Qwen3-Coder-Next activates 3 billion parameters and can run on a single GPU. That's the Civic. You want both in the garage.

**The distribution problem.** loa-finn wants to serve agents to many users simultaneously. Arrakis wants to token-gate agent access per community and per NFT. If every agent invocation requires a Claude Code session, horizontal scaling means spinning up Claude Code instances — which is both expensive and architecturally fragile. A provider-abstracted model layer lets loa-finn route requests to a pool of self-hosted models, managed APIs, or a hybrid of both.

> **Metaphor:** Right now, Loa is a restaurant where every dish is cooked by one Michelin-star chef. What we need is a kitchen brigade — the chef still handles the tasting menu, but the sous chef handles prep, the pastry chef handles desserts, and the line cooks handle the lunch rush. The diners don't need to know who cooked their meal. They just need it to be good.

---

## 2. Architecture Overview

### 2.1 The Five-Layer Model

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     AGENT DEFINITION LAYER                       │
│  Skills (SKILL.md) · Personas · Protocols · Memory               │
│  ↕ Model-agnostic. No provider references. Pure intent.          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                     MODEL ROUTING LAYER                           │
│  Provider Registry (Hounfour) · Agent↔Model Binding · Middleware │
│  ↕ Reads config, resolves model per agent, enforces budgets      │
│  ↕ Selects execution mode: native_runtime OR remote_model        │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                     MODEL ADAPTER LAYER (Cheval)                 │
│  cheval.py — unified Python adapter core                         │
│  ↕ Config resolution, request building, response normalization   │
│  ↕ Tool call translation, thinking trace extraction, metering    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                     INFRASTRUCTURE LAYER                          │
│  Self-hosted (vLLM/SGLang) · Managed APIs · Cloud GPU clusters   │
│  ↕ Prometheus metrics, health checks, circuit breakers           │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                     DISTRIBUTION LAYER (Arrakis)                 │
│  Token-gating · Per-NFT routing · Tenant billing · Rate limits   │
│  ↕ Users access agents through Arrakis; Arrakis delegates to     │
│    loa-finn; loa-finn delegates to the model layer               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 2.2 The Full Request Path

```
  User (Discord/Telegram/Web)
       │
       ▼
  ┌─────────┐
  │ Arrakis │──── Token-gate check (ownsNFT? hasTier?)
  └────┬────┘    Tenant ID injected (signed JWT, never raw headers)
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────┐
  │ loa-finn │──── Session management, WAL, compound learning
  └────┬─────┘    Selects agent, loads persona
       │
       ▼
  ┌────────────┐
  │  Hounfour  │──── Provider registry resolves agent→model binding
  │  (Router)  │    Budget check, capability check
  │            │    Execution mode: native_runtime OR remote_model
  └─────┬──────┘
        │
   ┌────┴────────────────────────────────┐
   │                                      │
   ▼ [native_runtime]                    ▼ [remote_model]
┌──────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────┐
│ Claude Code  │               │    cheval.py          │
│ in-process   │               │    (Python adapter)   │
│ SKILL.md     │               │    OpenAI-compat wire │
│ execution    │               └──────┬───────┬────────┘
└──────┬───────┘                      │       │
       │                    ┌─────────┘       └──────────┐
       │                    ▼                             ▼
       │          ┌──────────────────┐         ┌──────────────────┐
       │          │ External APIs    │         │ Self-Hosted      │
       │          │ OpenAI/Moonshot  │         │ vLLM/SGLang      │
       │          └────────┬─────────┘         └────────┬─────────┘
       │                   │                            │
       └───────────────────┼────────────────────────────┘
                           │
               ┌───────────▼───────────┐
               │    Metering Layer     │
               │  JSONL ledger         │
               │  Prometheus scraping  │
               │  Per-tenant billing   │
               └───────────────────────┘
```

---

## 3. Model Catalog

### 3.1 The Roster

| Alias | Canonical ID | Architecture | Active Params | Context | Thinking | Tool Calling | Primary Role |
|-------|-------------|-------------|--------------|---------|----------|-------------|-------------|
| `native` | `claude-code:session` | Dense | Full | 200k | Yes | Full runtime | Implementation, architecture |
| `reasoning` | `moonshot:kimi-k2-thinking` | MoE (1T total) | 32B | 256k | Yes | Native | Deep reasoning, Flatline challenger |
| `fast-code` | `qwen-local:qwen3-coder-next` | MoE (80B total) + DeltaNet | 3B | 256k | No | Native | Fast coding, light tasks |
| `reviewer` | `openai:gpt-4o` | Dense | Full | 128k | No | Yes | Code review, Flatline primary |
| `cheap` | `openai:gpt-4o-mini` | Dense | Full | 128k | No | Yes | Summaries, translations |

> **Note on naming:** Marketing names (Kimi K2 Thinking, Qwen3-Coder-Next) differ from model IDs used in API calls (`kimi-k2-thinking`, `Qwen3-Coder-Next`). The canonical ID column uses the exact string passed to the provider API. Aliases are Loa-internal shorthand and always resolve to a `provider:model-id` pair. The `pricing` section must key on the same provider names used in `providers`.

### 3.2 Qwen3-Coder-Next — The Self-Hosting Sweet Spot

> *"Think of it like this: Kimi-K2 is a freight train — enormous capacity, enormous infrastructure to run. Qwen3-Coder-Next is an electric scooter — it gets you where you need to go, costs almost nothing, and fits in your apartment."*

This model changes the economics of self-hosting entirely:

- **80B total parameters, 3B activated per token.** The MoE architecture means only 3.75% of the model fires on any given forward pass. Same efficiency trick that made Google's Switch Transformer viable at scale.
- **Hybrid DeltaNet/Attention architecture.** 48 layers: `12 × (3 × (Gated DeltaNet → MoE) → 1 × (Gated Attention → MoE))`. DeltaNet layers handle sequential state with linear attention (O(n)), traditional attention layers handle long-range dependencies.
- **Native tool calling with `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`** in both SGLang and vLLM. First realistic open-source candidate for a non-Claude `implementing-tasks` agent.
- **256k native context.** Matches Kimi-K2, exceeds GPT-4o.
- **Apache 2.0 license.** No restrictions on commercial use.
- **Runs on 2× A100 (or 1× RTX 4090 for local dev).** Compare to Kimi-K2's 8-32× H100. Infrastructure cost difference: 10-50×.

**Deployment:**
```bash
# SGLang (recommended)
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-Next \
  --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 2 \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder

# vLLM
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-Next \
  --port 8000 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder
```

### 3.3 Kimi-K2-Thinking — The Reasoning Heavyweight

1T parameter MoE, 32B active per token. Key differentiator: exposes `reasoning_content` in API responses — unlike OpenAI o-series which hides reasoning. For the Flatline Protocol, you can audit *why* the challenger disagreed, not just *that* it disagreed.

**Hardware requirements (illustrative — verify against provider pricing pages before committing):**

| Configuration | Hardware | VRAM Required | Approx. Cost/hr |
|--------------|----------|---------------|-----------------|
| FP8 production | 8× H100 80GB | ~1TB | $24-80/hr |
| INT4 minimum | 4× H200 141GB | ~500GB | $15-42/hr |
| Quantized dev | 1× 24GB GPU + 256GB RAM | ~247GB total | ~$0 (owned), 1-2 tok/s |

**Recommendation:** Use the Moonshot API or HuggingFace Inference Providers. Self-hosting only makes sense above ~$5k/month in API spend.

### 3.4 Thinking Trace Normalization

| Provider | Source Field | Accessible? | Loa Normalized |
|----------|-------------|------------|----------------|
| Claude (native_runtime) | `thinking` blocks in content | Yes | `<thinking>...</thinking>` |
| Claude (remote_model via API) | `thinking` blocks in content | Yes | `<thinking>...</thinking>` |
| OpenAI o-series | `reasoning_content` | Hidden | Not accessible |
| Kimi-K2-Thinking | `reasoning_content` in message | **Yes** | `<thinking>...</thinking>` |
| Qwen3-Coder-Next | N/A | N/A (non-thinking model) | No thinking output |

> **FAANG Parallel:** This is the observability problem Uber faced with their heterogeneous microservice fleet. Different services emitted logs in different formats. The solution was Jaeger (now OpenTelemetry) — a unified trace format that normalizes across emitters. Our thinking trace normalization is the same pattern applied to LLM reasoning.

---

## 4. Prior Art & What We're Stealing

### 4.1 Vercel AI SDK — Provider Registry Pattern

The gold standard for multi-model abstraction in TypeScript. We adopt the `provider:model` string convention, provider registry as single source of truth, middleware for model-specific settings. We adapt it from compiled code into YAML config because Loa is shell-script + SKILL.md, not a TypeScript app.

### 4.2 OpenCode — Configuration Architecture

OpenCode is the most mature open-source multi-model agent CLI. Key patterns adopted:

| OpenCode Pattern | Loa Adaptation |
|-----------------|----------------|
| `{env:VAR}` variable substitution | Keeps secrets out of config files |
| `{file:path}` file inclusion | Load persona prompts from external files |
| `limit.context` / `limit.output` | Routing constraint — don't send 200k to a 32k model |
| Per-agent `model` override | Our `agent_bindings` |
| `enabled_providers` / `disabled_providers` | Restrict available models per project |
| Config precedence (remote → global → project) | Maps to Loa's Three-Zone Model |
| Model variants | Multiple configs for same model |
| Agent definition via JSON or markdown files | Matches our SKILL.md + persona decomposition |

### 4.3 Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)

Already established in Arrakis. The agent skill (domain logic) never knows or cares which model executes it. The port defines the contract; adapters handle provider-specific quirks.

---

## 5. Provider Abstraction Layer

### 5.1 The ModelPort Interface

The contract every adapter must satisfy. This is the **single authority** for what "talking to a model" means in Loa:

```typescript
interface ModelPort {
  // Core completion — blocking request/response
  complete(request: CompletionRequest): CompletionResult

  // Streaming completion — optional, degrades gracefully to complete()
  stream(request: CompletionRequest): AsyncStream<StreamChunk>

  // Static capabilities — declared in config, verified at health-check time
  capabilities(): ModelCapabilities

  // Health probe — used by circuit breaker
  healthCheck(): HealthStatus
}

// ─── Request Types ───────────────────────────────────────────

interface CompletionRequest {
  messages: Message[]
  tools?: ToolDefinition[]          // See §5.3 Tool Calling Contract
  options: {
    temperature?: number
    top_p?: number
    max_tokens?: number             // Clamped to min(requested, provider.limit.output)
    stop?: string[]
  }
  metadata: {
    agent: string                   // e.g., "reviewing-code"
    tenant_id?: string              // Injected by Arrakis
    nft_id?: string                 // Injected by Arrakis (finnNFT)
    trace_id: string                // UUID for request tracing
  }
}

interface Message {
  role: "system" | "user" | "assistant" | "tool"
  content: string | ContentBlock[]
  thinking?: string | null          // Normalized from reasoning_content / extended_thinking
  tool_calls?: ToolCall[] | null    // See §5.3
  tool_call_id?: string | null      // For role="tool" messages
}

// ─── Response Types ──────────────────────────────────────────

interface CompletionResult {
  content: string
  thinking: string | null           // Normalized thinking trace
  tool_calls: ToolCall[] | null     // Normalized tool calls (see §5.3)
  usage: {
    prompt_tokens: number
    completion_tokens: number
    reasoning_tokens: number        // 0 if not available
  }
  metadata: {
    model: string                   // Actual model used (from provider response)
    provider_request_id?: string    // Provider's request ID, if available
    latency_ms: number
    trace_id: string                // Echoed from request
  }
}

interface ModelCapabilities {
  tool_calling: boolean
  thinking_traces: boolean
  max_context: number
  max_output: number
  vision: boolean
  streaming: boolean
}

interface HealthStatus {
  healthy: boolean
  latency_ms: number
  error?: string
}
```

### 5.2 Execution Modes

The router does not treat all models the same. There are two fundamentally different execution modes, and routing must choose between them explicitly:

**Mode 1: `native_runtime`**

The agent runs inside Claude Code's process. Claude Code provides file system access, tool execution, REPL integration, and the full agentic runtime. The "model" is the running Claude instance itself.

- Only applicable to provider type `claude-code`.
- The `implementing-tasks` agent currently *requires* this mode (file writes, test execution, tool use against the local workspace).
- `model-invoke` is NOT called. The Loa slash command dispatches directly to Claude Code, which loads the SKILL.md.
- Metering: captured by wrapping the Claude Code session with pre/post hooks that extract token counts from the session transcript.

**Mode 2: `remote_model`**

The agent's persona is sent as a system prompt to an HTTP-accessible model. The model returns text (and optionally tool calls / thinking traces). The model has no file system access unless the adapter implements an agentic tool-call loop.

- Applicable to provider types: `openai`, `openai-compatible`.
- All non-Claude agents use this mode.
- `model-invoke` dispatches to `cheval.py`, which handles config resolution, request building, response normalization, and metering.

**Routing resolution:**

```
resolve_execution_mode(agent, binding):
  provider_type = config.providers[binding.provider].type
  
  if provider_type == "claude-code":
    return native_runtime
  else:
    # Check: does agent REQUIRE native_runtime?
    if agent.requires.native_runtime:
      ERROR: "Agent {agent} requires native_runtime but is bound to {binding}"
    return remote_model
```

> **For Future Agents:** This two-mode split is deliberate and should be preserved. The temptation will be to unify everything into remote_model by wrapping Claude Code in an HTTP adapter. Resist this until Phase 5 — the native runtime's tool integration is fundamentally richer than what you can replicate over HTTP. Google learned this with GFS vs Colossus: sometimes the "special" path exists because the semantics genuinely differ, not because someone was lazy.

### 5.3 Tool Calling Contract

The tool calling surface is where "OpenAI-compatible" diverges most between providers. The adapter layer normalizes all tool interactions to the following canonical shapes:

**5.3.1 Tool Definition (request → provider)**

Loa's normalized tool definition:

```json
{
  "type": "function",
  "function": {
    "name": "search_codebase",
    "description": "Search for code patterns across the repository",
    "parameters": {
      "type": "object",
      "required": ["query"],
      "properties": {
        "query": {
          "type": "string",
          "description": "Search query (regex or plain text)"
        },
        "file_pattern": {
          "type": "string",
          "description": "Glob pattern to filter files (e.g., '*.ts')"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

This is the OpenAI tools format. Adapters translate to provider-specific formats where necessary:

| Provider | Tools Format | Adapter Responsibility |
|----------|-------------|----------------------|
| OpenAI | Native — pass through | None |
| Moonshot/Kimi-K2 | OpenAI-compatible | None (pass through) |
| Qwen3-Coder-Next (vLLM/SGLang) | OpenAI-compatible with `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder` | None (server-side parsing) |
| Claude API (remote_model) | Anthropic format (different structure) | Translate: `tools[].function` → `tools[].input_schema` |

**5.3.2 Tool Call in Response (provider → Loa normalized)**

Loa's normalized `ToolCall`:

```json
{
  "id": "call_abc123",
  "type": "function",
  "function": {
    "name": "search_codebase",
    "arguments": "{\"query\": \"ModelPort\", \"file_pattern\": \"*.ts\"}"
  }
}
```

| Provider | Response Shape | Adapter Translation |
|----------|---------------|-------------------|
| OpenAI | `choices[0].message.tool_calls[]` | Direct map |
| Kimi-K2 | `choices[0].message.tool_calls[]` | Direct map |
| Qwen3-Coder-Next | `choices[0].message.tool_calls[]` | Direct map (with `--tool-call-parser`) |
| Claude API | `content[].type == "tool_use"` → `{id, name, input}` | Translate: `.input` → `.function.arguments` (JSON-stringified) |

**5.3.3 Tool Result Message (Loa → provider)**

When the caller has a tool result to feed back:

```json
{
  "role": "tool",
  "tool_call_id": "call_abc123",
  "content": "{\"results\": [{\"file\": \"src/port.ts\", \"line\": 42, \"match\": \"interface ModelPort\"}]}"
}
```

| Provider | Expected Shape | Adapter Translation |
|----------|---------------|-------------------|
| OpenAI | `role: "tool"`, `tool_call_id`, `content` | Direct map |
| Kimi-K2 / Qwen3 | Same as OpenAI | Direct map |
| Claude API | `role: "user"`, content block `{type: "tool_result", tool_use_id, content}` | Translate: `role` → `user`, wrap in content block |

**5.3.4 Streaming with Tool Calls (Phase 3+)**

When streaming is enabled, tool calls arrive as deltas:

```json
// OpenAI-style streaming chunk with tool call delta
{
  "choices": [{
    "delta": {
      "tool_calls": [{
        "index": 0,
        "id": "call_abc123",           // Only in first chunk
        "type": "function",             // Only in first chunk
        "function": {
          "name": "search_codebase",    // Only in first chunk
          "arguments": "{\"quer"        // Partial JSON, accumulated across chunks
        }
      }]
    }
  }]
}
```

The adapter accumulates streaming tool call chunks and emits a complete `ToolCall` only when the tool call is fully assembled. Partial tool calls are never exposed to the routing layer.

**5.3.5 Tool Calling Modes**

The adapter supports three tool calling modes per request:

| Mode | Meaning | Config |
|------|---------|--------|
| `auto` | Model decides whether to call tools | `tool_choice: "auto"` |
| `required` | Model must call at least one tool | `tool_choice: "required"` |
| `none` | Tools are provided for context but model must not call them | `tool_choice: "none"` |

**Portability matrix:**

| Mode | OpenAI | Moonshot/Kimi-K2 | vLLM | SGLang |
|------|--------|-----------------|------|--------|
| `auto` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |
| `required` | ✅ | ✅ | ⚠️ Partial (model-dependent) | ⚠️ May not be supported |
| `none` | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

**Adapter responsibility:** If the target provider does not support `tool_choice: "required"`, the adapter must:
1. Fall back to `tool_choice: "auto"`.
2. Log a warning: `"tool_choice 'required' not supported by {provider}, falling back to 'auto'"`.
3. Record the fallback in the response metadata so the orchestrator can decide whether to retry or accept.

The adapter must NOT fail the request due to unsupported `tool_choice`. This is a soft degradation, not a hard error. The orchestrator (loa-finn) can inspect the response and re-prompt if no tool calls were returned when they were expected.

> **For Future Agents:** The `arguments` field in `ToolCall` is always a JSON string, not a parsed object. This is deliberate — it matches the OpenAI wire format and avoids double-parse bugs. The caller is responsible for `JSON.parse(tool_call.function.arguments)`.

**5.3.6 Tool-Call Loop Ownership**

`cheval.py` **never executes tools.** It only translates and normalizes tool-call schemas. The ownership split:

| Responsibility | Owner | Why |
|---------------|-------|-----|
| Translate tool definitions into provider format | `cheval.py` | Wire-protocol concern |
| Send tools in request, receive tool_calls in response | `cheval.py` | HTTP concern |
| Normalize tool_calls into Loa canonical format | `cheval.py` | Adapter concern |
| **Execute tools** (file writes, searches, API calls) | **loa-finn orchestrator** | Sandbox, ACLs, quotas, audit |
| Format tool results into tool_result messages | `cheval.py` (on next call) | Wire-protocol concern |

This means a multi-step tool-calling agent works as follows:

```
loa-finn                         cheval.py                    Provider
   │                                │                            │
   ├─── invoke(agent, prompt) ─────▶│                            │
   │                                ├── build request + tools ──▶│
   │                                │◀── response: tool_calls ───┤
   │◀── normalized tool_calls ──────┤                            │
   │                                │                            │
   ├── execute tools in sandbox ────┤                            │
   │   (ACL check, quota check)    │                            │
   │                                │                            │
   ├── invoke(agent, tool_results)─▶│                            │
   │                                ├── build follow-up ────────▶│
   │                                │◀── response: content ──────┤
   │◀── final content ─────────────┤                            │
```

loa-finn controls the loop, the sandbox, and the number of iterations. `cheval.py` is stateless between calls.

### 5.4 Capability Matrix

Capabilities are the source of truth for routing decisions. They live in config, can be optionally verified by health probes, and are checked before every dispatch.

**5.4.1 Declared Capabilities (config is authority)**

```yaml
# In each model definition within a provider
models:
  gpt-4o:
    capabilities:
      tool_calling: true
      thinking_traces: false
      vision: true
      streaming: true
    limit:
      context: 128000
      output: 16384
```

**5.4.2 Required Capabilities (per agent)**

```yaml
agents:
  implementing-tasks:
    model: native
    requires:
      native_runtime: true     # Cannot run as remote_model
      tool_calling: true
  
  reviewing-code:
    model: reviewer
    requires:
      tool_calling: false      # Text-only analysis
      thinking_traces: optional # Nice to have, not required
  
  flatline-challenger:
    model: reasoning
    requires:
      thinking_traces: required # Must have reasoning traces
      tool_calling: false
```

**5.4.3 Resolution Algorithm**

```
dispatch(agent, binding):
  model = resolve_alias(binding)
  caps  = config.providers[model.provider].models[model.id].capabilities
  reqs  = config.agents[agent].requires
  limit = config.providers[model.provider].models[model.id].limit
  
  // Hard failures
  if reqs.native_runtime and model.type != "claude-code":
    FAIL "Agent requires native_runtime"
  if reqs.tool_calling == true and caps.tool_calling != true:
    FAIL "Agent requires tool_calling, model does not support it"
  if reqs.thinking_traces == "required" and caps.thinking_traces != true:
    FAIL "Agent requires thinking_traces, model does not support it"
  
  // Soft clamps
  effective_max_output = min(request.max_tokens, limit.output)
  
  // Dispatch
  if model.type == "claude-code":
    return dispatch_native(agent)
  else:
    return dispatch_remote(agent, model, effective_max_output)
```

> **For Future Agents:** The capability check happens at routing time, not at request time. This means a misconfigured binding (e.g., routing a tool-calling agent to a model without tool support) fails immediately at startup or config validation, not silently at 3am during a sprint.

### 5.5 Adapter Implementations

Three adapters, unified by `cheval.py`:

| Adapter | Provider Type | Wire Protocol | Notes |
|---------|-------------|---------------|-------|
| `NativeRuntimeAdapter` | `claude-code` | In-process / CLI | Wraps Claude Code session; captures output + usage from session transcript |
| `OpenAIAdapter` | `openai` | OpenAI Chat Completions | Standard OpenAI, direct pass-through |
| `OpenAICompatAdapter` | `openai-compatible` | OpenAI Chat Completions | Covers Moonshot, HF, vLLM, SGLang, Ollama, Docker Model Runner |

All HTTP-based adapters (OpenAI + OpenAI-compat) share the same request-building and response-normalization code in `cheval.py`. The only differences are endpoint URL, auth headers, and minor response field mapping (e.g., `reasoning_content` extraction for Kimi-K2).

### 5.6 Skill Decomposition for Portability

```
.claude/skills/reviewing-code/
├── SKILL.md              # Claude Code entry point (native_runtime wrapper)
├── persona.md            # Model-agnostic persona → becomes system prompt for remote_model
├── evaluation-criteria.md # What this agent evaluates
└── output-schema.md      # Expected output format (for validation)
```

`remote_model` reads `persona.md` as system prompt + `output-schema.md` as formatting instruction. `native_runtime` uses `SKILL.md` which wraps everything. Zero breakage on the native path.

---

## 6. Configuration Schema

### 6.1 Naming Rules

The `provider:model` convention must be consistent everywhere. These rules are enforced by config validation.

**Rule 1: Always `provider:model-id`.** Even for Claude Code: `claude-code:session`. The alias `native` resolves to `claude-code:session`.

**Rule 2: Provider keys in config match provider keys in pricing.** If the provider is called `moonshot` in `providers`, it must be called `moonshot` in `pricing`. Not `anthropic` in one and `claude` in the other.

**Rule 3: Model IDs match the string sent to the API.** If the Moonshot API expects `kimi-k2-thinking`, that's the model ID. Not a marketing name, not a slug.

**Rule 4: Aliases are Loa-internal shorthand.** They resolve to `provider:model-id` pairs. Aliases never appear in API calls.

| Layer | Example | Where It Appears |
|-------|---------|-----------------|
| Alias | `reasoning` | `.loa.config.yaml` agent bindings only |
| Canonical ID | `moonshot:kimi-k2-thinking` | Resolved by router, passed to adapter |
| API model string | `kimi-k2-thinking` | Sent in HTTP request body `"model": "..."` |
| Marketing name | Kimi K2 Thinking | Documentation only, never in config or code |

### 6.2 Precedence & Merge Semantics

**Precedence (lowest → highest):**

```
1. System Zone defaults    (.claude/defaults/model-config.yaml)
2. Global user config      (~/.loa/config.yaml)
3. Project config          (.loa.config.yaml in project root)
4. CLI override            (--model moonshot:kimi-k2-thinking)
5. Environment variables   (LOA_MODEL=qwen-local:qwen3-coder-next)
```

**Merge rules:**

| Config Type | Merge Behavior | Example |
|-------------|---------------|---------|
| `providers` (map) | **Deep merge.** Higher-precedence adds or overrides individual providers. A project config can add `qwen-local` without replacing `openai` from global. | Global has `openai`, project adds `qwen-local` → both available |
| `providers.*.models` (map) | **Deep merge.** New models added, existing model keys override. | Global defines `gpt-4o`, project overrides its `limit.output` |
| `aliases` (map) | **Shallow merge.** Higher-precedence replaces individual alias values. | Global: `fast-code: qwen-local:...`, project: `fast-code: qwen-cloud:...` → project wins |
| `agents` (map) | **Deep merge.** Higher-precedence overrides individual agent fields. | Global sets `reviewing-code.model: reviewer`, project sets `reviewing-code.temperature: 0.1` → both applied |
| `pricing` (map) | **Deep merge.** Project can override prices for specific models. | |
| `enabled_providers` (array) | **Replace.** Higher-precedence array replaces entirely. | |
| `disabled_providers` (array) | **Replace.** Higher-precedence array replaces entirely. | |
| `metering.budgets` (map) | **Shallow merge.** Individual budget keys override. | |
| Scalars (`default_model`, etc.) | **Replace.** Higher-precedence wins. | |

**Variable interpolation:**

- `{env:VAR_NAME}` — resolved **after merge**. The highest-precedence config layer wins the value, then the env var reference is resolved. Empty string if env var is not set. Error if env var is referenced but critical (API key for an enabled provider).
- `{file:path/to/file}` — resolved **before merge, per-layer**. Path is relative to the directory containing that config file. So `{file:prompts/system.md}` in `~/.loa/config.yaml` resolves relative to `~/.loa/`, while the same reference in `.loa.config.yaml` resolves relative to the project root. Absolute paths are also accepted. Error if file not found.
- **`cheval.py` handles all interpolation**, not bash. The implementation must track which config file each `{file:}` reference originated from during the merge phase.

### 6.3 The Full Config Schema

```yaml
# .loa.config.yaml v2
# Variable substitution: {env:VAR_NAME}, {file:path/to/file}
# Naming convention: provider keys and pricing keys MUST match

# ─── PROVIDERS ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
providers:
  claude-code:
    type: claude-code
    # No config — uses ambient Claude Code session
    models:
      session:
        name: "Claude Code (native runtime)"
        capabilities:
          tool_calling: true
          thinking_traces: true
          vision: true
          streaming: true
        limit: { context: 200000, output: 64000 }

  openai:
    type: openai
    options:
      baseURL: "https://api.openai.com/v1"    # Always explicit, always includes /v1
      apiKey: "{env:OPENAI_API_KEY}"
      timeout: 300000
    models:
      gpt-4o:
        name: "GPT-4o"
        capabilities: { tool_calling: true, thinking_traces: false, vision: true, streaming: true }
        limit: { context: 128000, output: 16384 }
      gpt-4o-mini:
        name: "GPT-4o Mini"
        capabilities: { tool_calling: true, thinking_traces: false, vision: false, streaming: true }
        limit: { context: 128000, output: 16384 }

  moonshot:
    type: openai-compatible
    options:
      baseURL: "https://api.moonshot.ai/v1"   # Always includes /v1
      apiKey: "{env:MOONSHOT_API_KEY}"
    models:
      kimi-k2-thinking:
        name: "Kimi K2 Thinking"
        capabilities: { tool_calling: true, thinking_traces: true, vision: false, streaming: true }
        limit: { context: 256000, output: 8192 }
        defaults: { temperature: 1.0, top_p: 0.95 }
      kimi-k2.5:
        name: "Kimi K2.5"
        capabilities: { tool_calling: true, thinking_traces: true, vision: true, streaming: true }
        limit: { context: 256000, output: 8192 }

  qwen-local:
    type: openai-compatible
    options:
      baseURL: "http://localhost:30000/v1"     # Always includes /v1
    models:
      qwen3-coder-next:
        name: "Qwen3 Coder Next (3B active / 80B total)"
        capabilities: { tool_calling: true, thinking_traces: false, vision: false, streaming: true }
        limit: { context: 256000, output: 65536 }
        defaults: { temperature: 1.0, top_p: 0.95 }

  huggingface:
    type: openai-compatible
    options:
      baseURL: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1"
      apiKey: "{env:HF_TOKEN}"
    models:
      moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Instruct-0905:
        name: "Kimi K2 via HuggingFace"
        capabilities: { tool_calling: true, thinking_traces: true, vision: false, streaming: true }
        limit: { context: 256000, output: 8192 }

# ─── ALIASES ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
aliases:
  native: "claude-code:session"
  reasoning: "moonshot:kimi-k2-thinking"
  fast-code: "qwen-local:qwen3-coder-next"
  reviewer: "openai:gpt-4o"
  cheap: "openai:gpt-4o-mini"

# ─── DEFAULT ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
default_model: native

# ─── AGENT CONFIGURATION ──────────────────────────────────────
agents:
  implementing-tasks:
    model: native
    requires: { native_runtime: true, tool_calling: true }

  reviewing-code:
    model: reviewer
    temperature: 0.3
    persona: .claude/skills/reviewing-code/persona.md
    requires: { tool_calling: false, thinking_traces: optional }

  flatline-challenger:
    model: reasoning
    requires: { thinking_traces: required, tool_calling: false }

  translating-for-executives:
    model: fast-code
    temperature: 0.7
    requires: { tool_calling: false }

  # (remaining agents follow the same pattern)
  discovering-requirements: { model: native }
  designing-architecture:   { model: native }
  planning-sprints:         { model: native }
  auditing-security:        { model: native }
  deploying-infrastructure: { model: native }
  flatline-primary:         { model: reviewer }
  bridgebuilder:
    model: reviewer
    temperature: 0.3
    persona: .claude/skills/bridgebuilder/persona.md
    requires: { tool_calling: false }

# ─── ROUTING: FALLBACK & DOWNGRADE ─────────────────────────────
routing:
  # Fallback chains (availability — provider is down)
  # Ordered list: try first, then second, etc.
  # Resolution filters by: enabled_providers, agent.requires capabilities
  fallback:
    "moonshot:kimi-k2-thinking":
      - "huggingface:moonshotai/Kimi-K2-Instruct-0905"
      - "openai:gpt-4o"
    "qwen-local:qwen3-coder-next":
      - "openai:gpt-4o-mini"
    "openai:gpt-4o":
      - "moonshot:kimi-k2-thinking"

  # Downgrade chains (cost — budget pressure)
  # Orthogonal to fallback. Only triggered by budget enforcement.
  # Resolution ALSO filters by agent.requires capabilities.
  downgrade:
    "claude-code:session": ["openai:gpt-4o", "qwen-local:qwen3-coder-next", "openai:gpt-4o-mini"]
    "openai:gpt-4o":       ["qwen-local:qwen3-coder-next", "openai:gpt-4o-mini"]
    "moonshot:kimi-k2-thinking": ["openai:gpt-4o", "openai:gpt-4o-mini"]

  # Health check config
  health:
    interval_seconds: 30
    timeout_ms: 5000
    unhealthy_threshold: 3        # Consecutive failures before circuit opens
    recovery_threshold: 1         # Successes before circuit closes
    # Default probe — works for self-hosted (vLLM, SGLang)
    # COMPOSITION RULE: probe_url = baseURL + probe_path
    # Since baseURL already includes /v1, probe paths must NOT include /v1.
    # For host-relative paths (e.g., SGLang /health), set host_relative: true
    # which strips the /v1 suffix from baseURL before composing.
    default_probe:
      path: "/models"             # → baseURL + /models → .../v1/models
      method: GET
      requires_auth: false
    # Provider-specific probe overrides
    provider_probes:
      openai:
        path: "/models"           # → https://api.openai.com/v1/models
        method: GET
        requires_auth: true       # Needs Bearer token
        interval_seconds: 60      # Probe less often (rate limit risk)
      moonshot:
        path: "/models"           # → https://api.moonshot.ai/v1/models
        method: GET
        requires_auth: true
        interval_seconds: 60
      qwen-local:
        path: "/health"           # SGLang native health (host-level, no /v1 prefix)
        method: GET
        requires_auth: false
        host_relative: true       # Compose as baseURL.rstrip("/v1") + path
                                  # → http://localhost:30000/health
    # Circuit breaker state storage
    state_backend: in_process     # Phase 0-2: per-instance memory
                                  # Phase 3+: "redis" for shared state across replicas
    redis_url: "{env:LOA_REDIS_URL}"  # Only used when state_backend: redis

# ─── PROVIDER RESTRICTIONS ─────────────────────────────────────
enabled_providers: []       # Empty = all enabled
disabled_providers: []      # Explicitly block specific providers

# ─── METERING ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
metering:
  enabled: true
  ledger_path: loa-grimoire/a2a/cost-ledger.jsonl
  budgets:
    per_phase: "$5.00"
    per_sprint: "$25.00"
    per_project: "$200.00"
  alerts:
    warn_at_percent: 80
    block_at_percent: 100
  on_budget_exceeded: warn       # "warn" | "block" | "downgrade"

  # Scope identification — tells budget enforcement what "current phase" means.
  # These are resolved from (in priority order):
  #   1. CLI args (--phase, --sprint, --project)
  #   2. loa-finn session metadata (if running inside loa-finn)
  #   3. Environment variables (LOA_PROJECT_ID, LOA_PHASE_ID, LOA_SPRINT_ID)
  #   4. Config defaults below
  scope:
    project_id: "{env:LOA_PROJECT_ID}"    # Required for budget enforcement
    phase_id: "{env:LOA_PHASE_ID}"        # Optional — scopes per_phase budget
    sprint_id: "{env:LOA_SPRINT_ID}"      # Optional — scopes per_sprint budget

  # Ledger rotation — prevents unbounded file growth in long-running deployments.
  # Phase 0-2: local JSONL with rotation.
  # Phase 3+: optionally ship to object store / log pipeline (S3, Loki, ClickHouse).
  ledger_rotation:
    max_size_mb: 50                       # Rotate when file exceeds this size
    max_age_days: 30                      # Rotate files older than this
    archive_path: loa-grimoire/a2a/archive/  # Rotated files moved here
    # Phase 3+ optional: ship to external pipeline
    # export_to: "s3://loa-metering/{project_id}/{date}/"

# ─── PRICING ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Keys MUST match provider names in `providers` section.
# Per 1M tokens, USD. Treat as illustrative — maintain a
# separate pricing.yaml or script that pulls current rates.
pricing:
  openai:
    gpt-4o:          { input: 2.50, output: 10.00, cached_input: 1.25 }
    gpt-4o-mini:     { input: 0.15, output: 0.60,  cached_input: 0.075 }
  moonshot:
    kimi-k2-thinking: { input: 1.00, output: 3.00 }
  claude-code:
    session:          { input: 3.00, output: 15.00, cached_input: 0.30 }
  qwen-local:
    qwen3-coder-next:
      type: gpu-hourly
      gpu_cost_per_hour: 3.00
      estimated_throughput_tok_s: 200

# ─── DATA RETENTION ────────────────────────────────────────────
# See §10 for full policy
retention:
  store_prompts: false              # Never store raw prompts by default
  store_responses: false            # Never store raw responses by default
  store_thinking_traces: false      # Ephemeral by default
  thinking_trace_opt_in: per_phase  # "never" | "per_phase" | "always"
  redaction:
    enabled: true
    patterns:
      - "(?i)(api[_-]?key|secret|token|password)\\s*[:=]\\s*\\S+"
      - "\\b[A-Za-z0-9._%+-]+@[A-Za-z0-9.-]+\\.[A-Z|a-z]{2,}\\b"
```

### 6.4 Routing: Fallback & Downgrade

Two orthogonal mechanisms handle two different failure modes:

**Fallback (availability):** The preferred provider is unreachable. The circuit breaker opens after `unhealthy_threshold` consecutive probe failures. The router walks the fallback chain, skipping any entry that doesn't satisfy the agent's `requires` capabilities or is in `disabled_providers`.

**Downgrade (cost):** Budget enforcement triggers a switch to a cheaper model. The router walks the downgrade chain, skipping any entry that doesn't satisfy `requires`. If the agent has `requires.native_runtime: true`, downgrade is **impossible** (cannot downgrade away from Claude Code to a remote model).

```
resolve_with_fallback_and_downgrade(agent, binding):
  model = resolve_alias(binding)
  
  // Cost check first
  if budget_exceeded(agent) and config.metering.on_budget_exceeded == "downgrade":
    for candidate in config.routing.downgrade[model]:
      if satisfies_requirements(candidate, agent.requires):
        model = candidate
        LOG "Budget downgrade: {agent} → {candidate}"
        break
  
  // Availability check
  if not health_check_ok(model):
    for candidate in config.routing.fallback[model]:
      if satisfies_requirements(candidate, agent.requires) and health_check_ok(candidate):
        model = candidate
        LOG "Fallback: {agent} → {candidate}"
        break
    else:
      FAIL "No healthy provider available for {agent}"
  
  return model
```

---

raw.body:
# RFC: The Hounfour — Multi-Model Provider Abstraction, Cloud Deployment & Agent Distribution

**Status:** Draft v4 — Implementation-Ready (blocking fixes applied)  
**Author:** Jani  
**Date:** 2026-02-08  
**Revision:** v3 addressed operational items; v4 fixes five blocking correctness issues from final review  
**Scope:** Loa Framework → loa-finn Runtime → Arrakis Distribution  
**References:** [finnNFT #27](https://github.com/0xHoneyJar/loa-finn/issues/27) · [Bridgebuilder #24](https://github.com/0xHoneyJar/loa-finn/issues/24) · [OpenCode Config](https://opencode.ai/docs/config/)

---

## Preamble: Why This Document Exists

> *"The difference between a junior engineer and a senior engineer is that the junior asks 'does it work?' and the senior asks 'what happens when it works at scale, for 10,000 users, at 3am, when the primary model provider is down?'"*

Three systems are converging:

1. **Loa** — an AI agent-driven development framework with 8 specialized agents, currently coupled to Claude Code as both runtime and model.
2. **loa-finn** — an OpenCode-like service that gives Loa a server runtime: persistent sessions, scheduled behaviors, compound learning, and a tool sandbox. Think of it as the engine block.
3. **Arrakis** — a token-gated community management platform spanning Discord and Telegram. Think of it as the highway system.

The vision: Loa agents run inside loa-finn, served to users through Arrakis, powered by whichever model backend is cheapest, fastest, or most capable for the task. A finnNFT holder talks to their daemon companion — and behind the scenes, the personality prompt routes to Qwen3-Coder-Next for a quick code fix, Kimi-K2-Thinking for deep multi-step reasoning, or Claude for architecture decisions. The user never knows. The NFT doesn't care. The wallet just sees a bill.

This RFC defines the complete architecture for that future: from the provider abstraction in Loa, through the cloud deployment in loa-finn, to the metered distribution through Arrakis.

---

## Table of Contents

1. [The Problem](#1-the-problem)
2. [Architecture Overview](#2-architecture-overview)
3. [Model Catalog](#3-model-catalog)
4. [Prior Art & What We're Stealing](#4-prior-art--what-were-stealing)
5. [Provider Abstraction Layer](#5-provider-abstraction-layer)
    - 5.1 The ModelPort Interface
    - 5.2 Execution Modes
    - 5.3 Tool Calling Contract
    - 5.4 Capability Matrix
    - 5.5 Adapter Implementations
    - 5.6 Skill Decomposition for Portability
6. [Configuration Schema](#6-configuration-schema)
    - 6.1 Naming Rules
    - 6.2 Precedence & Merge Semantics
    - 6.3 The Full Config Schema
    - 6.4 Routing: Fallback & Downgrade
7. [Adapter Implementation](#7-adapter-implementation)
    - 7.1 model-invoke (shell orchestrator)
    - 7.2 cheval.py (Python adapter core)
    - 7.3 File Map
8. [Cloud Deployment](#8-cloud-deployment)
9. [Metering, Billing & Cost Attribution](#9-metering-billing--cost-attribution)
10. [Data Retention, Privacy & Thinking Trace Policy](#10-data-retention-privacy--thinking-trace-policy)
11. [Security & Multi-Tenant Hardening](#11-security--multi-tenant-hardening)
12. [Agent Distribution via Arrakis](#12-agent-distribution-via-arrakis)
13. [Repo Ownership](#13-repo-ownership)
14. [Implementation Phases](#14-implementation-phases)
15. [Design Decisions & Rationale](#15-design-decisions--rationale)
16. [Open Questions](#16-open-questions)
17. [Success Criteria](#17-success-criteria)
18. [Naming & Mythology](#18-naming--mythology)

---

## 1. The Problem

Loa is currently a one-model framework. Every agent — from the requirements discoverer to the security auditor — runs on Claude Code. The GPT integration in the Flatline Protocol is ad-hoc, bolted on with direct API calls rather than flowing through a principled abstraction.

This creates three problems:

**The vendor lock problem.** If Anthropic's API goes down, every agent goes down. If pricing doubles, every agent's cost doubles. Google learned this with their early dependence on a single ad-serving stack — when they finally built the Universal Second Price auction to abstract across formats, revenue diversification followed. We need our agents to be model-portable.

**The cost problem.** Claude Opus at $75/1M output tokens is a Lamborghini. Beautiful, but you don't drive it to the grocery store. Some tasks — summarizing a sprint for executives, generating a quick unit test — need a Honda Civic. Qwen3-Coder-Next activates 3 billion parameters and can run on a single GPU. That's the Civic. You want both in the garage.

**The distribution problem.** loa-finn wants to serve agents to many users simultaneously. Arrakis wants to token-gate agent access per community and per NFT. If every agent invocation requires a Claude Code session, horizontal scaling means spinning up Claude Code instances — which is both expensive and architecturally fragile. A provider-abstracted model layer lets loa-finn route requests to a pool of self-hosted models, managed APIs, or a hybrid of both.

> **Metaphor:** Right now, Loa is a restaurant where every dish is cooked by one Michelin-star chef. What we need is a kitchen brigade — the chef still handles the tasting menu, but the sous chef handles prep, the pastry chef handles desserts, and the line cooks handle the lunch rush. The diners don't need to know who cooked their meal. They just need it to be good.

---

## 2. Architecture Overview

### 2.1 The Five-Layer Model

```
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     AGENT DEFINITION LAYER                       │
│  Skills (SKILL.md) · Personas · Protocols · Memory               │
│  ↕ Model-agnostic. No provider references. Pure intent.          │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                     MODEL ROUTING LAYER                           │
│  Provider Registry (Hounfour) · Agent↔Model Binding · Middleware │
│  ↕ Reads config, resolves model per agent, enforces budgets      │
│  ↕ Selects execution mode: native_runtime OR remote_model        │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                     MODEL ADAPTER LAYER (Cheval)                 │
│  cheval.py — unified Python adapter core                         │
│  ↕ Config resolution, request building, response normalization   │
│  ↕ Tool call translation, thinking trace extraction, metering    │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                     INFRASTRUCTURE LAYER                          │
│  Self-hosted (vLLM/SGLang) · Managed APIs · Cloud GPU clusters   │
│  ↕ Prometheus metrics, health checks, circuit breakers           │
├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                     DISTRIBUTION LAYER (Arrakis)                 │
│  Token-gating · Per-NFT routing · Tenant billing · Rate limits   │
│  ↕ Users access agents through Arrakis; Arrakis delegates to     │
│    loa-finn; loa-finn delegates to the model layer               │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### 2.2 The Full Request Path

```
  User (Discord/Telegram/Web)
       │
       ▼
  ┌─────────┐
  │ Arrakis │──── Token-gate check (ownsNFT? hasTier?)
  └────┬────┘    Tenant ID injected (signed JWT, never raw headers)
       │
       ▼
  ┌──────────┐
  │ loa-finn │──── Session management, WAL, compound learning
  └────┬─────┘    Selects agent, loads persona
       │
       ▼
  ┌────────────┐
  │  Hounfour  │──── Provider registry resolves agent→model binding
  │  (Router)  │    Budget check, capability check
  │            │    Execution mode: native_runtime OR remote_model
  └─────┬──────┘
        │
   ┌────┴────────────────────────────────┐
   │                                      │
   ▼ [native_runtime]                    ▼ [remote_model]
┌──────────────┐               ┌──────────────────────┐
│ Claude Code  │               │    cheval.py          │
│ in-process   │               │    (Python adapter)   │
```

### 3.2 Qwen3-Coder-Next — The Self-Hosting Sweet Spot

> *"Think of it like this: Kimi-K2 is a freight train — enormous capacity, enormous infrastructure to run. Qwen3-Coder-Next is an electric scooter — it gets you where you need to go, costs almost nothing, and fits in your apartment."*

This model changes the economics of self-hosting entirely:

- **80B total parameters, 3B activated per token.** The MoE architecture means only 3.75% of the model fires on any given forward pass. Same efficiency trick that made Google's Switch Transformer viable at scale.
- **Hybrid DeltaNet/Attention architecture.** 48 layers: `12 × (3 × (Gated DeltaNet → MoE) → 1 × (Gated Attention → MoE))`. DeltaNet layers handle sequential state with linear attention (O(n)), traditional attention layers handle long-range dependencies.
- **Native tool calling with `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`** in both SGLang and vLLM. First realistic open-source candidate for a non-Claude `implementing-tasks` agent.
- **256k native context.** Matches Kimi-K2, exceeds GPT-4o.
- **Apache 2.0 license.** No restrictions on commercial use.
- **Runs on 2× A100 (or 1× RTX 4090 for local dev).** Compare to Kimi-K2's 8-32× H100. Infrastructure cost difference: 10-50×.

**Deployment:**
```bash
# SGLang (recommended)
python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-Next \
  --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 2 \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder

# vLLM
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-Coder-Next \
  --port 8000 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 2 \
  --enable-auto-tool-choice \
  --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder
```

### 3.3 Kimi-K2-Thinking — The Reasoning Heavyweight

1T parameter MoE, 32B active per token. Key differentiator: exposes `reasoning_content` in API responses — unlike OpenAI o-series which hides reasoning. For the Flatline Protocol, you can audit *why* the challenger disagreed, not just *that* it disagreed.

**Hardware requirements (illustrative — verify against provider pricing pages before committing):**

| Configuration | Hardware | VRAM Required | Approx. Cost/hr |
|--------------|----------|---------------|-----------------|
| FP8 production | 8× H100 80GB | ~1TB | $24-80/hr |
| INT4 minimum | 4× H200 141GB | ~500GB | $15-42/hr |
| Quantized dev | 1× 24GB GPU + 256GB RAM | ~247GB total | ~$0 (owned), 1-2 tok/s |

**Recommendation:** Use the Moonshot API or HuggingFace Inference Providers. Self-hosting only makes sense above ~$5k/month in API spend.

### 3.4 Thinking Trace Normalization

| Provider | Source Field | Accessible? | Loa Normalized |
|----------|-------------|------------|----------------|
| Claude (native_runtime) | `thinking` blocks in content | Yes | `<thinking>...</thinking>` |
| Claude (remote_model via API) | `thinking` blocks in content | Yes | `<thinking>...</thinking>` |
| OpenAI o-series | `reasoning_content` | Hidden | Not accessible |
| Kimi-K2-Thinking | `reasoning_content` in message | **Yes** | `<thinking>...</thinking>` |
| Qwen3-Coder-Next | N/A | N/A (non-thinking model) | No thinking output |

> **FAANG Parallel:** This is the observability problem Uber faced with their heterogeneous microservice fleet. Different services emitted logs in different formats. The solution was Jaeger (now OpenTelemetry) — a unified trace format that normalizes across emitters. Our thinking trace normalization is the same pattern applied to LLM reasoning.

## 4. Prior Art & What We're Stealing

### 4.1 Vercel AI SDK — Provider Registry Pattern

The gold standard for multi-model abstraction in TypeScript. We adopt the `provider:model` string convention, provider registry as single source of truth, middleware for model-specific settings. We adapt it from compiled code into YAML config because Loa is shell-script + SKILL.md, not a TypeScript app.

### 4.2 OpenCode — Configuration Architecture

OpenCode is the most mature open-source multi-model agent CLI. Key patterns adopted:

| OpenCode Pattern | Loa Adaptation |
|-----------------|----------------|
| `{env:VAR}` variable substitution | Keeps secrets out of config files |
| `{file:path}` file inclusion | Load persona prompts from external files |
| `limit.context` / `limit.output` | Routing constraint — don't send 200k to a 32k model |
| Per-agent `model` override | Our `agent_bindings` |
| `enabled_providers` / `disabled_providers` | Restrict available models per project |
| Config precedence (remote → global → project) | Maps to Loa's Three-Zone Model |
| Model variants | Multiple configs for same model |
| Agent definition via JSON or markdown files | Matches our SKILL.md + persona decomposition |

### 4.3 Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters)

Already established in Arrakis. The agent skill (domain logic) never knows or cares which model executes it. The port defines the contract; adapters handle provider-specific quirks.
